d.title: The same OVER clause, with and without an ORDER BY inside it
d.caption: **PARTITION BY divides the rows exactly as GROUP BY would — and then does not collapse them.** That is the whole difference, and it is why a window can put the customer's total on every one of that customer's rows, ready to compare against the row's own amount. **Adding an ORDER BY inside the same OVER changes the aggregate from a partition total to a running total**, restarting at each new customer. Several windows with different partitions and orders can sit in one SELECT, each computed independently, from a single scan of the data.

d.title: Why a row can be compared with its own group
d.caption: **The window value sits on the row, which is the one thing GROUP BY cannot give you** — so salary minus the department average is an ordinary subtraction rather than a join back to an aggregated copy of the table. That is the class of question windows exist for: per-row against its own group. **The WINDOW clause is worth using as soon as two functions share a definition:** it names the window once, so the query shortens and the planner sorts once for all of them rather than once each.

d.title: Three ranking functions, one tie, three different answers to top three
d.caption: **In engineering the third and fourth salaries tie, and that single fact makes the three functions disagree about how many rows top-three means.** ROW_NUMBER hands out 3 and 4 arbitrarily and returns exactly three rows; RANK gives both the tied rows 3 and returns four; DENSE_RANK does the same without leaving a gap afterwards. **Only the question can say which is right** — “exactly three bonuses to award” and “everyone in the top three salary bands” are different requirements. And ROW_NUMBER without a tie-breaker is non-deterministic: add the primary key as the last ORDER BY column.

d.title: ROWS counts rows; RANGE measures the sort key
d.caption: **Three rows back is not the same amount of time on two different days** — which is the whole reason RANGE exists. Over a timestamp, a 30-day RANGE frame is genuinely “every order in the 30 days up to this one”, so orders drop out of the window as they age rather than as new rows arrive. Over a number it becomes a value band. **And the behaviour that surprises everyone: rows with the same sort value are always in a RANGE frame together**, so a running total over a non-unique key jumps by the whole tied group at once. RANGE is the default, which is why this bites unasked.

d.title: LAG reads the previous row, which is only the previous month if no month is missing
d.caption: **Group to months first, then LAG the revenue by one — and the whole correctness of that depends on every month having a row.** A month with no orders produces no row, so LAG silently compares March against January and reports a change that never happened. A date spine with zeros is what makes “previous row” mean “previous month”. **The other discipline is leaving the first month NULL:** there is no previous period, which is a different fact from a change of zero, and coalescing it to 0 puts a false flat month at the start of every chart.

d.title: Flag, running-sum, group: one shape for two different questions
d.caption: **A running COUNT(DISTINCT) is not available — engines refuse it, because the frame would have to remember every earlier value** — and the workaround is the same three-step shape that solves streaks. For cumulative customers: assign each one to the month they first appeared, count first appearances per month, running-sum that. **For growth streaks: flag the months that did not grow, running-sum the flags, and every row sharing a flag total is one streak.** Learning this shape once covers gaps-and-islands, sessionisation and streaks — they are the same query.
